standard.title: Similarities and differences between target language and English using metalanguage
standard.description: reflect on and explain similarities and differences between the target language and English language structures and features, using metalanguage
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can compare language structures and features across the target language and English using metalanguage, and produce comparative analyses (AC9LCH6U03). They have compared text types, grammar and cohesive devices. They have not yet taught younger students using comparative frameworks, explored metaphorical versus literal meaning across languages, or applied comparative understanding to unlock unfamiliar content.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students reflect on and explain similarities and differences between the target language and English across a range of text types and grammatical features — using metalanguage to extend and apply comparative understanding, including to unfamiliar content and to support others' learning.

nodes.label: Extended metalanguage for text and grammar analysis
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use extended metalanguage to describe and explain a range of text-level and grammatical features in both the target language and English.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least six metalanguage terms correctly across a text or grammar analysis that covers both languages, including at least one text-level term (e.g. paragraph, cohesion, point of view) and one grammatical term.
nodes.typical_width: Use extended metalanguage for text features — paragraphing, conjunctions, sequencing, point of view, descriptive and emotive language; compare how these features work in target language and English texts; read formal texts such as reports and news articles and compare with own everyday speech.
wider: Annotate a target language text fully using metalanguage for every grammatical and textual feature — compare the annotation with an English equivalent and identify all structural differences
Create a metalanguage comparison resource for a specific feature that differs across the two languages — designed to be used by another learner
nodes.hinge_reason: Extended metalanguage is the prerequisite for systematic language comparison and for supporting others' language learning. Students who cannot name and describe language features cannot explain similarities and differences, cannot apply comparative knowledge to unfamiliar content, and cannot teach others.

response_modes.reason: Metalanguage is built through repeated deployment across varied analysis tasks — not through a single lesson. Students need to encounter and use each metalanguage term across multiple text types and comparison contexts before it becomes functional analytical vocabulary.

success_criteria: Uses at least six metalanguage terms correctly across a text or grammar analysis
Includes at least one text-level and one grammatical metalanguage term used accurately

nodes.label: Metaphorical and literal meaning across languages
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify and compare metaphorical and literal meaning in target language and English texts, and explain how metaphor functions differently across the two languages.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples of metaphorical language in the target language, explain the literal and metaphorical meanings, and compare with English equivalents or absence of equivalents.
nodes.typical_width: Explore metaphorical and literal meaning in target language texts; compare metaphorical expressions across target language and English; identify where the same metaphor exists in both languages and where languages use different metaphors for the same concept; apply understanding to interpret unfamiliar metaphorical content.
wider: Research a specific conceptual metaphor that operates differently in the target language and English — explain how each language encodes the concept and what this reveals about cultural thinking
Analyse a target language text rich in metaphor — identify every metaphorical expression, explain its meaning, and compare with how English would express the same idea

response_modes.reason: Metaphorical meaning analysis requires students to hold both literal and figurative readings simultaneously and compare these across two language systems. Explicit scaffolding — identifying the literal meaning first, then the figurative, then comparing — builds this dual-level analysis capacity.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Metaphor analysis is an intellectually rich domain where background learners' bilingual knowledge gives them genuine analytical advantage. Width investment here develops a sophisticated understanding of how language encodes thought — a transferable analytical capability beyond the language classroom.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two metaphorical expressions in the target language with explanations of literal and figurative meanings
Compares at least one with the English equivalent or explains why English handles the concept differently

nodes.label: Applying comparative knowledge to support learning
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can apply comparative language knowledge to access unfamiliar content and to support younger learners' understanding of key language differences.
nodes.minimum_width: Apply comparative language knowledge to access at least one unfamiliar text, explaining the strategies used, and produce at least one resource or explanation for a younger learner about a key language difference.
nodes.typical_width: Apply understanding of text and grammar features to access unfamiliar content in target language and English; teach younger students about key differences using support resources; compare content development across text types; apply comparative understanding to analyse public texts such as news articles.
wider: Create a teaching resource for younger learners about a specific language difference — test it with a real or simulated audience and revise based on feedback
Apply comparative linguistic knowledge to analyse a genuinely unfamiliar text type in the target language — document the strategies used and evaluate their effectiveness

response_modes.reason: Applying comparative knowledge to support learning integrates metalanguage command (node 1) and metaphor analysis (node 2) into a teaching and transfer task. The teaching investment is in creating genuine transfer conditions — real unfamiliar content, real younger learners — that require students to apply their knowledge functionally.

success_criteria: Applies comparative knowledge to access at least one unfamiliar text, explaining strategies used
Produces a resource or explanation for a younger learner about at least one key language difference
